repository.title: MATLAB Simulink Energy Lab
repository.description: Run reduced-order battery, thermal, converter and BESS control models with transparent equations and repeatable testing.
repository.summary: The native repository contains Base MATLAB and generated Simulink models for batteries, thermal response, converters, and BESS control. A second-order response exercise develops control intuition before the bounded native examples.
repository.audience: Electrical-engineering students, MATLAB users, and researchers studying reproducible reduced-order models.

model.equation: y″ + 2ζωₙy′ + ωₙ²y = Kωₙ²r. Closed-form unit-step response is evaluated for underdamped, critical, and overdamped regimes.
assumptions: A linear time-invariant second-order system starts at rest.
No transport delay, saturation, sensor noise, or discrete controller is represented.
Overshoot is relative to the final K·r level; tracking error remains relative to the requested r.
The 20-second response is deliberately rescaled for learning; it does not use the native converter’s electrical constants or subsecond scenario.
No MATLAB or Simulink engine is embedded in this page. Native scripts and toolbox requirements remain available through the source links.
Analytic agreement is numerical verification, not measured battery, inverter, grid-code, or hardware validation.
model.introduction: The browser uses an ideal linear second-order system, not the repository’s actual buck-converter, EKF, or BESS controller. Use it to predict damping and gain effects before inspecting the native saturation, sample-time, and validation contracts.

modules.title: Predict a control response from its equation
modules.objective: Identify target, damping, natural frequency, and gain in a small dynamic model.
steps: Read the native closed-loop converter engineering question and its two state equations.
Apply a 60-unit step with damping 0.5, natural frequency 1 rad/s, and unit gain.
Predict overshoot and final tracking before running the deliberately slower browser response.

checkpoints.label: Theoretical overshoot for the initial damping

modules.reflection: Which native converter states, actuator limits, and sample-time choices are absent from this ideal response?

modules.title: Change response speed while keeping damping
modules.objective: Distinguish natural frequency from damping and steady-state gain.
steps: Keep the step, gain, and damping fixed; double natural frequency to 2 rad/s.
Compare the response at two seconds and the theoretical overshoot.
Read the model-selection guide and identify a native model suitable for a converter-control question.

checkpoints.label: Faster system output after two seconds

modules.reflection: Why does doubling a natural frequency in this toy not justify doubling controller gains in the native plant?

modules.title: Use a limiting case as a verification check
modules.objective: Explain the value and scope of an analytic reference case.
steps: Set damping to 1, frequency to 1 rad/s, and keep unit gain.
Predict a monotonic critical response and inspect the one-second and final outputs.
Find the Base MATLAB check entry point and distinguish a no-plot regression from a displayed figure.

checkpoints.label: Critical response has no theoretical overshoot
Final tracking error is below 0.01 unit

modules.reflection: What would a deterministic passing check establish, and what independent measurement evidence would still be missing?

modules.title: Choose the smallest defensible native model
modules.objective: Carry an explicit control question into the repository’s model and validation map.
steps: Apply gain 0.8 with damping 0.7 and natural frequency 1.5 rad/s.
Predict the nonzero steady-state error even though the response is well damped.
Use the native converter and BESS limitations to write a study plan with inputs, limits, checks, expected outputs, and excluded claims.

checkpoints.label: Steady tracking error remains about 12 units

modules.reflection: Which extension—saturation, measurement bias, discrete timing, or grid transition—requires a richer native model, and why?
